sources.title: Stephen Wilkes: The passing of time, caught in a single photo – TED-Vortrag (Transkript)
sources.excerpt: My process begins by photographing iconic locations, places that are part of what I call our collective memory. I photograph from a fixed vantage point, and I never move. I capture the fleeting moments of humanity and light as time passes.
sources.author: Stephen Wilkes

sources.title: Stephen Wilkes: The passing of time, caught in a single photo – TED-Vortrag (Transkript)
sources.excerpt: So once I decide on my view and the location, I have to decide where day begins and night ends. And that's what I call the time vector.

sources.excerpt: What I discovered with the Hudson River School was that these artists were painting light moving; it was not just a scene, but the light, depth, and three-dimensional quality made it very unique.

sources.title: Stephen Wilkes: The passing of time, caught in a single photo – TED-Vortrag (Transkript)
sources.excerpt: Photographing for anywhere from 15 to 30 hours and shooting over 1,500 images, I then choose the best moments of the day and night. Using time as a guide, I seamlessly blend those best moments into one single photograph, visualizing our conscious journey with time.
sources.author: Stephen Wilkes

sources.title: In Discussion: Stephen Wilkes „Beyond the Horizon“ – Holden Luntz Gallery (Vortragsmitschrift)
sources.excerpt: People often ask me, “How do you even pay attention for that long?” What I do is almost like a deep meditation.

sources.excerpt: Dombrovskis’s preferred camera was the Linhof Master Technika. Requiring 4 x 5 inch film, almost 16 times larger than that used in a standard 35mm camera, the Linhof was heavy and cumbersome, forcing Dombrovskis to take more care and time in setting up his shots and making each of these images the result of physical and mental endurance, as well as involved decision-making.

sources.title: Review: ‘Dombrovskis: journeys into the wild’, Monash Gallery of Art – Art Blart (Marcus Bunyan, mit Ausstellungstexten, 2019)
sources.excerpt: Dombrovskis’s images demonstrate nature’s powerful splendour but they also have a quiet, reflective quality that draws the viewer into an intimate conversation with the natural world. This is, perhaps, achieved through his habit of including the unexpected and sensitive details within a landscape, as well as the marvellous and dramatic vistas.
sources.author: Monash Gallery of Art (Ausstellungstext)

sources.title: Ragnar Axelsson – Overview, Qerndu Gallery & Publishing
sources.excerpt: In stark black-and-white images, he captures the elemental, human experience of nature at the edge of the liveable world, making visible the extraordinary relationships between the people of the Arctic and their extreme environment - relationships now being altered in profound and complex ways by unprecedented climate changes.
sources.author: Qerndu Gallery

sources.title: Ragnar Axelsson: At the Edge of the World – The Photographers’ Gallery, London (2024/25)
sources.excerpt: Axelsson immerses himself in Arctic communities for weeks, earning the trust and friendship necessary to portray the unguarded realities of their everyday lives. “I write down what people say and how they feel; I try to capture that in their eyes,” Axelsson explains.
sources.author: The Photographers’ Gallery

sources.title: Ragnar Axelsson – Greenland, Kunstfoyer München (Ausstellungstext, Qerndu)
sources.excerpt: Working with  black-and-white images , Ragnar cuts the Arctic down to its raw essence: ice, wind, darkness, animals, mountains and human faces. His photographs carry both beauty and menace.
sources.author: Qerndu Gallery

sources.title: Ragnar Axelsson: At the Edge of the World – The Photographers’ Gallery, London (2024/25)
sources.excerpt: Hunting communities in the Arctic are integral to the cultural and social fabric of the North. Having passed down centuries-old traditions, the once-reliable sea ice now shifts unpredictably, reshaping hunting grounds and upending daily life for communities that depend on it.
sources.author: The Photographers’ Gallery

sources.title: About Ken Duncan – Website des Fotografen
sources.excerpt: In the early 1980s, while working as a senior technical representative for one of Australia's leading photographic companies, Ken encountered a piece of equipment that would change his life - the Widelux panoramic camera. For the first time, he could translate onto film the expansive, sweeping vistas exactly as he experienced them.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Website)

sources.title: About Ken Duncan – Website des Fotografen
sources.excerpt: A landscape can change from beautiful to breathtaking in a single moment - when a prism of light breaks through the clouds, when the rising sun peeks over the horizon, when a shadow's arc changes to dramatic effect. Light changes everything.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Website)

sources.title: About Ken Duncan – Website des Fotografen
sources.excerpt: Then there are other times when patience is required - long periods of silence and contemplation watching the natural world slowly change, until a moment of light transforms everything.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Website)

sources.title: About Ken Duncan – Website des Fotografen
sources.excerpt: In 1982, driven by conviction rather than certainty, Ken left the security of his career in Sydney and set out across Australia. His goal was simple yet ambitious: to create a book that would reveal the true spirit of the nation.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Website)

sources.title: About Ken Duncan – Website des Fotografen
sources.excerpt: For Ken Duncan, one such moment came with the release of his first major book, The Last Frontier - Australia Wide in 1987. At a time when panoramic photography was virtually unheard of in publishing, the book broke new ground and met with remarkable success.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Website)

sources.title: Ken Duncan: Dawn of Creation, Mitchell Falls – Bildseite mit Text des Fotografen (kenduncan.com)
sources.excerpt: While camping at Mitchell Falls in the western Kimberley we were surrounded throughout the night by fires lit by National Park authorities to aid the germination of bush seed. This form of environmental care has been practised by Aborigines for millennia. As smoke tempered the early morning light with lovely evenness, the colours of rock and water began to glow.
sources.author: Ken Duncan

sources.title: Ken Duncan: Full Moon, Bungle Bungles – Bildseite mit Text des Fotografen (kenduncan.com)
sources.excerpt: A full moon rises over the Bungle Bungles in Western Australia, its soft, caressing light enhancing the subtleties of colour and texture that are highlighted by the golden afterglow of the dying sun.
sources.author: Ken Duncan (Bildtext)

sources.title: Ken Duncan: Heart of a Nation, Uluru – Bildseite mit Text des Fotografen (kenduncan.com)
sources.excerpt: Behind me, the horizon was covered in cloud, and just when I thought to pack up my gear, light suddenly found its way through a hole in the clouds and produced a wonderful show for me to capture on film.

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Bredicot Church – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Turner is best known for his bold and large-scale (30 x 40 cm) albumen prints from calotype negatives showing rural English scenes in the picturesque tradition: ruined abbeys, castles, farmhouses and the rural landscape.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Torquay – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: His images result from a long exposure time (up to thirty minutes), which means that many of the negatives do not show any figures or animals.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Torquay – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: The paper fibres of the paper also produced a distinctive aesthetic when developing images: it makes them slightly rough, with a grainy texture that seems to be a good fit for Turner's photographs of rural scenes.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Hedgerow Trees, Clerkenleap – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Between 1852 and 1854 Turner compiled 60 of his own photographs, including this one, in what is believed to be a unique album, 'Photographic Views from Nature'.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Crowle Court – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Emulating the generation of watercolour painters before him, he sought out old buildings and quiet landscapes across England that were full of 'picturesque' possibilities – rich textures and contrasting tones, often at historical locations in a state of decay.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Hedgerow Trees, Clerkenleap – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Figures in contemporary dress would have made Turner's photographs historically specific; without figures they have a timeless quality.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Hedgerow Trees, Clerkenleap – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: This is the only photograph in Turner's album to include a human figure, seen here leaning against a fence and a pollarded oak tree. The figure may be Turner himself.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Hurtmore Lane – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: As with so many of his photographs in rural areas, the focus was on the picturesque possibilities of lanes, trees and agricultural equipment.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Pepperharrow Park – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Here he has chosen an old and picturesque tree as his central motif, so the photograph has the character of a portrait.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Windmill, Kempsey – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: In the 19th century, windmills were being made redundant by the bigger, new steam-driven mills. Hence Turner was recording a rapidly disappearing feature of the English agricultural landscape.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Eashing Bridge – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: Although the bridge itself was of great historic interest, Turner seems to have been equally absorbed in the intricate pattern of the trees.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Rivaulx Abbey – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: It was one of a number of abandoned and ruinous abbeys in Yorkshire that became a favourite subject for visiting artists in the 18th century and later.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: Crowle Court – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: The site must once have been of importance, since it was surrounded by a defensive moat, visible to the right of the raised entrance roadway. This ancient building, which seems to grow out of its surrounding terrain, was a typical subject for Benjamin Brecknell Turner.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Benjamin Brecknell Turner: At Compton – Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Objekttext)
sources.excerpt: This photograph gives us a great deal of information about the agricultural cycle: a large corn rick, indicative of that summer's good harvest, can be seen on the left.
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

sources.title: Malcolm Daniel: Édouard Baldus – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs (nach dem Heilbrunn-Essay des Metropolitan Museum)
sources.excerpt: He was recognized as one of the few photographers to combine aesthetic sensitivity with an astonishing technical prowess in the still experimental and handcrafted medium.
sources.author: Malcolm Daniel

sources.title: Malcolm Daniel: Édouard Baldus – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs (nach dem Heilbrunn-Essay des Metropolitan Museum)
sources.excerpt: In 1851 he was one of five artists selected by the Commission des monuments historiques, a government agency, to carry out missions héliographiques, photographic surveys of the nation’s architectural patrimony.
sources.author: Malcolm Daniel

projects.title: Album Chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée (1861; Auswahl Landschaften)

sources.title: Malcolm Daniel: Édouard Baldus – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs (nach dem Heilbrunn-Essay des Metropolitan Museum)
sources.excerpt: But it was in the second of his two railway albums, commissioned in 1861 by the Chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée, that Baldus again pioneered new aesthetic ground. The album is a masterfully composed sequence of sixty-nine photographs of the landscape, towns, principal sites of interest, and railroad structures along the line from Lyon to Marseille and Toulon.
sources.author: Malcolm Daniel

sources.title: Malcolm Daniel: Édouard Baldus – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs (nach dem Heilbrunn-Essay des Metropolitan Museum)
sources.excerpt: And his presentation of a landscape transformed by modern engineering confidently espoused a belief in technological progress.
sources.author: Malcolm Daniel

sources.title: Bisson Frères – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs
sources.excerpt: Sons of a heraldic painter who experimented with the daguerreotype, Louis-Auguste Bisson (French, 1814-1876) and his brother Auguste-Rosalie Bisson (French, 1826-1900) often collaborated throughout their photographic careers as “Bisson Frères”, one of the best known and prolific photographic firms of the period.
sources.author: Hans P. Kraus Jr.

sources.title: Bisson Frères – Biography, Hans P. Kraus Jr. Fine Photographs
sources.excerpt: Their large photographs of Chartres from the late 1850s focus on a selected group of details using dramatic lighting to deepen the shadows and enhance the sculptural quality. By 1860, they were making breathtaking views high up in the Alps.
sources.author: Hans P. Kraus Jr.

sources.title: Bisson Frères: Glacier des Bossons – The American Museum of Photography
sources.excerpt: Their most famous body of work is comprised of the high-altitude photographs they made in the Alps during the climbing seasons of 1859-1862. In 1860, on the occasion of the reunion of Savoy with France, and accompanied by Napoleon III and the Empress, the Bissons went to Chamonix to attempt the ascent of Mont-Blanc. They failed to reach the summit but the large glass negatives they produced during the climb were the basis of an album of twenty-four superb Alpine views.
sources.author: The American Museum of Photography

sources.title: Bisson Frères: Glacier des Bossons – The American Museum of Photography
sources.excerpt: Despite the arduous conditions, the Bissons captured this masterful scene of an epic struggle by men intent on conquering nature–set against a magnificent landscape.
sources.author: The American Museum of Photography

sources.title: Maxime Du Camp: ‘Egypte, Nubie, Palestine et Syrie’, 1852 – Christie’s, Losbeschreibung
sources.excerpt: Maxime Du Camp, a journalist, first travelled to the Orient in 1844-45 and published a written journal of his experiences, Souvenirs et paysages d'Orient , in 1848. His fascination with the Near East persisted and in 1849 he returned to Egypt, accompanied by his friend, the writer Gustave Flaubert.
